title: Tree: Height of a Binary Tree
directAnswer: Height is the number of EDGES on the longest root-to-leaf path — not nodes. The recursive answer: height = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), but with the base case set so a null child contributes −1, which makes a single leaf return 0. The clean trick most people use: treat a null node as height −1, so leaf = 1 + max(−1, −1) = 0. Either way it's postorder DFS in O(n) time and O(h) stack space.

remember.pattern: Postorder DFS aggregation, edge-counted (height, not depth)
rules: HackerRank counts **edges**, so a single node has height **0**, not 1.
The cleanest base case is `null → -1`; then a leaf evaluates to `1 + max(-1, -1) = 0`.
It's **postorder**: both children must report before the parent can answer.
Take the **max** of child heights (longest path), then **+1** for the edge to this node.
Don't confuse height (edges, this problem) with depth (nodes, LeetCode 104) — they differ by exactly 1.
whenToUse: You need the height (edge count) of a tree or longest root-to-leaf path
Any value where a node's answer is built bottom-up from its children
A building block for Balanced Tree, Diameter, and Max Path Sum
antiSignals: You need depth in NODES → return 1 + max with null = 0 (LeetCode 104 convention)
You need per-level node lists → that's Level Order Traversal, not a single number
You need the path itself → carry the path, not just the count
remember.takeaway: Height is the edge-counted twin of maximum depth. The only difference from the node-counted version is the base value: null returns −1 here instead of 0. Internalize the postorder shape — children return a value, parent folds with 1 + max.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know height is measured in edges (single node = 0) and can express it as a postorder aggregation where children compute before the parent.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning 1 for a single node — that's the node-counted depth, not the edge-counted height HackerRank wants. Off by one on every answer.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State up front that height counts edges, set the null base case to −1 so leaves naturally return 0, and note this is the same recursion as Maximum Depth shifted by one.

problemStatement:
The height of a binary tree is the number of **edges** between the tree's root and its furthest leaf.

Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its height.

For example, a tree with a single node has height `0`, because there are no edges below the root.
constraints: The tree is non-empty (at least the root exists)
Height is counted in edges, so a single node has height 0
understanding: Find the length, in edges, of the longest root-to-leaf path. This is the node-counting depth minus one. Because the input is always non-empty, we don't need an empty-tree case for the public function, but the recursion's null base case (−1) is what makes leaves resolve to 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is height measured in edges or nodes?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Edges. HackerRank's 'Height of a Binary Tree' returns 0 for a single node. If it counted nodes (LeetCode 104 depth), a single node would be 1. This shifts every answer by one.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The public input always has at least a root, so the function itself never sees an empty tree. But internally a null child is treated as height −1 so leaves return 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How deep can the tree get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 500 nodes, so a skewed tree is 500 deep — well within recursion limits in Java and Python.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do duplicate values matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Height depends only on structure, not on the values stored in the nodes.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS — 1 + max(left, right), null = −1 (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Start here. It's the textbook postorder one-liner; just be deliberate about the edge-counting base case.
hints: If you knew the height of the left subtree and the height of the right subtree, how would you get the height of the whole tree?
The height is 1 (for the edge down to a child) plus the taller of the two subtrees. What base value makes a single leaf come out as 0?
Set null → −1. Then a leaf computes 1 + max(−1, −1) = 0, exactly the edge-count definition. Recursive case: 1 + max(height(left), height(right)).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every node is visited once and does O(1) work (a max and an add) → O(n) time. Recursion depth equals tree height h → O(h) space: O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.
approaches.explanation:
Height has a naturally recursive definition: the height of a tree is one more than the height of its taller subtree, measured in edges.

**The base case is the whole trick.** A null child has no node and therefore contributes height −1. That negative value is deliberate: it makes a leaf node (two null children) evaluate to `1 + max(−1, −1) = 0`, which is exactly the edge-count height of a leaf. If you instead returned 0 for null, a leaf would report 1 and you'd be computing node-counted depth (LeetCode 104), off by one from what HackerRank asks.

**Recursive case.** For a real node, ask both children for their heights, take the larger (the longest path descends through the taller subtree), and add 1 for the edge connecting this node to that subtree.

**Why this is postorder.** A node cannot answer until *both* children have reported — the combining work happens on the way back up. That bottom-up shape is the most reused tree recursion: Balanced Tree, Diameter, and Maximum Path Sum are all this same structure with extra bookkeeping.

**Height vs depth in one sentence.** Height counts edges (this problem, null = −1, leaf = 0); depth counts nodes (LeetCode 104, null = 0, leaf = 1). Pick the base value to match the convention and the rest of the code is identical.
approaches.insight: The recursion returns *up* the tree. Each node waits for its children, then folds with 1 + max(...). The only knob between 'height' and 'depth' is the null base value (−1 vs 0) — choose it consciously and you'll never be off by one.

dryRun.input: root = [1,2,3,null,null,4,5] (1 has children 2 and 3; 3 has children 4 and 5)
dryRun.intro: Postorder: leaves resolve first (height 0), then parents add an edge. null returns −1.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def height(root: Node) -> int:
    if root is None:                                # null contributes -1 edge
        return -1
    return 1 + max(height(root.left),               # +1 edge to this node
                   height(root.right))              # children report first

java.explanation: Edge-count base case: a missing child is -1, so a leaf becomes 1 + max(-1,-1) = 0.
Children must finish before the parent — postorder ordering.
Longest path runs through the TALLER child; +1 counts the edge down to it.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS — Count Levels Minus One
approaches.whenToMention: Offer if the interviewer worries about recursion depth or wants an explicit-container version.
hints: Height in edges equals (number of levels) − 1. How would you count the levels of a tree without recursion?
Use a queue. Each outer iteration drains exactly one level; count how many levels you drain.
After the queue empties, subtract 1 from the level count to convert nodes-deep into edges-deep.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is enqueued and dequeued once → O(n) time. The queue holds at most one level, bounded by the maximum width w → O(w) space (up to O(n)).
approaches.explanation:
The number of edges on the longest path is one less than the number of levels, so a level-counting BFS answers it directly.

**The level-drain trick.** Seed a queue with the root and a level counter at 0. Each outer-loop iteration represents one level: snapshot the queue size, dequeue exactly that many nodes while enqueuing their children, then increment the level count. When the queue empties, the count is the number of levels.

**Converting to edges.** Levels counts nodes-deep (root level = 1). Height counts edges, which is one fewer, so the answer is `levels − 1`. For a single node we drain one level and return `1 − 1 = 0`, matching the edge convention.

**Why snapshot the size up front.** The queue grows as you enqueue children, so you must capture `levelSize` before the inner loop or you'd bleed into the next level. This 'capture the size, loop exactly that many times' idiom is the universal level-by-level BFS pattern.
approaches.insight: BFS gives you the level count for free; the only twist for height is subtracting 1 to convert nodes-deep into edges-deep. The same skeleton, keeping the popped values per level, becomes Level Order Traversal.

dryRun.intro: Drain one level per outer iteration, counting levels. Subtract 1 at the end for edges.

java.explanation: Snapshot BEFORE the inner loop so newly enqueued children don't inflate this level.
Increment once per LEVEL, not per node.
Levels counts nodes-deep; subtract 1 to get edges-deep height.

python.explanation: len(queue) captured at loop start fixes the level boundary.
One increment per fully drained level.
Convert level count into edge-counted height.

edgeCases.behavior: Queue peaks at the last level (~n/2 nodes) → O(n) space worst case.

pitfalls: Forgetting the −1 conversion and returning the node-counted depth.
Reading queue.size() inside the inner loop — bleeds levels together.
Incrementing levels per node instead of per level — wildly overcounts.

commonMistakes: Returning 1 for a single node (node-counted depth) instead of 0 (edge-counted height).
Setting the null base case to 0 instead of −1 in the edge-counting recursion.
Using min instead of max, yielding the shortest path.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting nodes instead of edges
commonMistakesDetailed.why: HackerRank's height is edges, so a single node is 0. Returning 0 for null makes a leaf return 1 (node-counted depth), off by one from the required answer.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using min instead of max
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Height follows the LONGEST root-to-leaf path. Using min returns the shortest path length, a different problem.

followupVariations.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: Same recursion but node-counted: null returns 0, so a single node is depth 1.

followupVariations.title: Balanced Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: Same height recursion, plus check |leftHeight − rightHeight| ≤ 1 at every node.

followupVariations.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: Track leftHeight + rightHeight at each node while the recursion returns the height upward.

patternNote: Postorder (bottom-up) aggregation, edge-counted. The height recursion is identical to the maximum-depth recursion except the null base case is −1 instead of 0, shifting every answer by one. This bottom-up shape — children return a value, parent folds with 1 + max — powers Balanced Tree, Diameter, and Max Path Sum.
